e.etymology: Coined for the heroine of the 2008 film 10,000 BC. Read backwards it spells te love, close to the love, and it also echoes Eve and Violet.
A modern American coinage joining Ty, as in Tyler and Tyson, to the -lin ending of Jaylin and Daylin.
A form of Annelie, a German and Swedish pet form of Anna and of Anneliese (Anna plus Elisabeth); in English it is also read as Anna plus Lee. Anna comes from Hebrew Hannah, grace.
A respelling of Kaia. In Scandinavia Kaia is a short form of Katarina; in the United States it is more often taken as a feminine form of Kai, Hawaiian for sea.
From Arabic safwan, a smooth bare rock, a word used in the Quran, from the root for what is pure and clear. Safwan ibn Umayya was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad.
From Arabic na'il, one who attains or wins, from the verb nala, to obtain. The spellings Nayel and Nael are common among Arabic-speaking families in France.
The form Spanish Bibles use for Adaiah, from Hebrew for the Lord has adorned, a name borne by several men in the Old Testament. In the US it is given to girls.
A respelling of Raven, the English bird name, from Old English hraefn. Raven took off as a girls' name in the late 1980s and 1990s, helped by actress Raven-Symoné.
A respelling of Kason, a modern American name that rhymes with Jason and Mason and overlaps with the surname Cason.
The Greek goddess of marriage and queen of Olympus, wife of Zeus; Juno is her Roman counterpart. The root of the name is uncertain, possibly akin to Greek heros, hero or protector.

assoc.t: Greek queen of the gods, wife of Zeus
Hera Syndulla, pilot in Star Wars Rebels and Ahsoka

e.etymology: From Arabic Rakan, steadfast or strong, from the root for something firm and dependable. It is especially common in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf.

assoc.t: Rakan, champion in the game League of Legends

e.etymology: The English word and surname, from Old English cniht, a youth or servant, later a mounted soldier of noble rank. As a first name it belongs with King, Prince and Duke.

assoc.t: the armored warrior of the Middle Ages and the chess piece

e.note: Sounds exactly like night, so it will often need spelling out.

e.etymology: A variant of Blakeley, an English surname from places named in Old English for a dark wood or clearing. The surname became a girls' name in the 2010s.
From Hebrew Zakkai, pure or innocent. It names a family that returned from exile in the books of Ezra and Nehemiah, and Zacchaeus is its Greek form.
An elaboration of Maeve with the -yn ending, also read as a respelling of Maven. Maeve is the English form of Irish Medb, intoxicating, the warrior queen of Connacht in Irish legend.
From Hebrew Hoshea, from the verb meaning to save. Hosea is the first of the twelve minor prophets of the Old Testament, and Joshua's name was Hoshea before Moses changed it.
namesakes: Hosea Williams (civil rights leader and aide to Martin Luther King Jr.)
Hosea Matthews (elder outlaw in the game Red Dead Redemption 2)

assoc.t: Book of Hosea in the Old Testament

e.etymology: A short form of Cyrus, the name of the Persian kings, and of Cyril, from Greek kyrios, lord. It has sometimes served for Seymour too.
namesakes: Cy Young (pitcher for whom baseball's top pitching award is named)

e.etymology: In Turkish, from sena, praise, a word borrowed from Arabic. Sena is also a Japanese name for girls and boys whose meaning depends on the kanji, and it was in American use in the 1880s.
A spelling of Aline, which began as a medieval short form of Adeline, from Germanic adal, noble. This spelling was at its most common in the US around 1900.
From Greek Theophilos, theos, god, plus philos, friend or beloved. Luke addresses his Gospel and the book of Acts to a Theophilus; Amadeus and Gottlieb translate the name into Latin and German.
namesakes: Theophilus (the reader addressed in Luke's Gospel and the book of Acts)

e.etymology: A modern coinage used mainly in Spanish-speaking families, putting a J on the sound of Ariel in the way Yariel does.
From Arabic fahd, cheetah or leopard. Fahd and Fahad are two spellings of the same name; King Fahd ruled Saudi Arabia from 1982 to 2005.
From Scottish Gaelic Alasdair, the Gaelic form of Alexander, from Greek for defender of men. Alastair is the spelling closest to the Gaelic; Alistair is the more common one in English.
The French word for cross, from Latin crux. As an American first name it comes by way of St. Croix, the Caribbean island and the river between Wisconsin and Minnesota.

assoc.t: St. Croix, largest of the US Virgin Islands

e.note: Americans say KROY, as in St. Croix and LaCroix sparkling water; the French word is KRWAH.

e.etymology: A form of Athaliah, Hebrew Atalyah, usually explained as the Lord is exalted. Atalia is the spelling of Spanish Bibles and of modern Hebrew.
e.note: The Biblical Athaliah was a queen of Judah who seized the throne by having her own grandsons killed.

e.etymology: From Arabic Mus'ab, from the root for difficult, used of a strong animal that is hard to tame. Mus'ab ibn Umayr was a companion of the Prophet Muhammad and Islam's first envoy to Medina.
From Arabic watin, the great artery that leaves the heart, a word found in the Quran. As a girls' name it carries the sense of someone as vital as one's own lifeblood.
A Spanish form of Raymond, more often spelled Raimundo, from the Germanic elements ragin, counsel, and mund, protection.
A respelling of Kinley, cut from the surname McKinley, Gaelic Mac Fhionnlaigh, son of Finlay. Finlay joins fionn, fair, and laoch, warrior.
A Yiddish-style spelling of Aharon, the Hebrew form of Aaron, the brother of Moses and first high priest of Israel. The root of the name is uncertain and may be Egyptian.
A respelling of Aaliyah, from Arabic aliya, high or exalted. Aaliyah became an American favorite through the R&B singer of that name in the 1990s.

e.meaning: fond remembrance of a loved one
e.etymology: From Hawaiian hali'a, a sudden fond memory, especially of a loved one. Halia was also a sea nymph of Rhodes in Greek myth, her name taken from hals, the sea.
